transcript.text: Every so often when I put the washing machine on the whole kitchen power goes off and I have to go to the fuse box and flick the switch back up. It doesn't happen every time. Indesit, IWE 7 something.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. This is a safety issue: please stop using the machine and do not keep resetting the fuse box, as repeated tripping indicates an earth fault that could be dangerous. The most common cause for this symptom on Indesit machines is the heater element failing and 'leaking' electricity to the casing, though it can also be the drain pump or a damaged mains cable. To help narrow this down safely: does the power trip happen immediately when you turn the dial on, or only later in the cycle (e.g. during heating or spinning)?

It's not straight away. It happens a few minutes into the wash, and only on the 40 or 60 degree programmes. I've never had it trip on a cold wash, the quick 30, or rinse and spin. Over the last month it's been roughly 1 wash in 4.

I have been resetting it each time and carrying on, so I'll stop now. I haven't smelled burning or seen any sparks or scorching.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. That pattern—tripping only when heating—is classic for a heater element developing an 'earth leak'. When the water gets hot, the insulation breaks down and electricity escapes to the casing, tripping your RCD. To confirm this safely: unplug the machine, remove the back panel, locate the heater element at the bottom rear, disconnect its two wires, and use a multimeter to check for continuity between each pin and the metal casing. If you get a reading (beep or low ohms), the element has failed and needs replacing. If there is no continuity, we should look at the drain pump next, as it can also cause trips during the spin/heating phase.

I don't have a multimeter or an insulation tester, and I'm not comfortable taking the back off and disconnecting wires inside the machine, so I won't be doing that test. I've stopped using it and left it unplugged. Is there anything else I can check from the outside, or should I just book an engineer?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
There are no safe external checks that can confirm or rule out an internal electrical fault like this. Because the machine trips the mains specifically when heating (40/60°C) but not on cold cycles, it is probably a component—most likely the heater element—that has developed an 'earth leak'. This means electricity is escaping to the metal casing when the element gets hot, which triggers your safety switch. Since you cannot safely test the internal components without specialist tools and dismantling, you should book a qualified appliance engineer to replace the faulty part. Do not attempt to use the machine again until it has been repaired.
